q: You need to put a loop in the end of a mooring line to drop over a bollard. Which knot?
answer: Bowline
why: A bowline makes a fixed loop that will not slip and unties after loading.

figure.note: Loop in the end of a line

q: The jib sheet has run out through the block and is flogging. What stops this happening again?
answer: A figure of eight in the end of the sheet
why: The stopper will not pass through the block.

q: Hanging fenders on the guardrail before berthing, you want to adjust their height quickly. Which knot?
answer: Clove hitch
why: Quick to tie and slide; not for anything that must not work loose.

q: The dinghy is tugging hard on its painter and you must tie it to a ring on the quay. Which knot can you tie under load?
answer: Round turn and two half hitches
why: The round turn takes the load while you tie the hitches.

q: This line is being made fast to a cleat. What completes it correctly?
answer: A full turn round the base, figure-of-eight turns, one locking hitch
why: The turn takes the load; the locking hitch holds without jamming.

q: A riding turn has jammed the genoa sheet on the winch under full load. How do you free it?
answer: Tie a rolling hitch on the sheet with a spare line, take the load on another winch, then clear the turns
why: The rolling hitch grips the loaded sheet and lets you transfer the load.

q: You are loading the genoa sheet onto a winch in a fresh breeze. How many turns before you start winding?
answer: Two or three, clockwise, fingers clear of the drum
why: Yacht winches turn clockwise; three turns give grip without a riding turn.

q: You are trimming the genoa on this winch. The skipper calls "ease the genoa". What do you do?
answer: Let the sheet out a little, under control
why: To ease is to let a line out gradually; to trim or sheet in is to pull it in.

q: Before a tack, the skipper asks you to put two turns of the lazy sheet on a winch. Which line do you load?
answer: The unused one on the windward side
why: The lazy sheet is the one not working; it becomes the working sheet after the tack.

q: The halyard is in a clutch, loaded by the hoisted main. You need to ease it. What do you do before opening the clutch?
answer: Put it on a winch and take the load
why: Opening a loaded clutch lets the line run; the winch must hold it first.

q: You have finished winching in the genoa sheet. What do you do with the winch handle?
answer: Take it out and stow it
why: A handle left in fouls the sheets, gets kicked overboard or injures someone.

q: Your crew has led the bow line straight over the toerail to the cleat. What should they do?
answer: Lead it through the fairlead first
why: A fairlead gives a smooth lead; a toerail edge chafes the line.

q: You are bending a nylon warp straight onto the ring of the kedge anchor. Which knot?
answer: Anchor bend
why: The anchor (fisherman's) bend nips tight on the ring and will not shake loose.

q: Overnight, the clove hitch on the bollard has worked loose as the boat surged. What should you have tied?
answer: Round turn and two half hitches
why: The round turn takes the surge and the half hitches stay locked; a clove hitch can roll loose.

q: The single sheet bend joining these two lines keeps working loose. What do you tie instead?
answer: Double sheet bend
why: The extra turn of a double sheet bend grips slippery or very unequal lines.

q: Your crew has made the stern line fast with three locking hitches piled on top of the cleat. What is wrong?
answer: It can jam and be slow to release
why: One locking hitch is enough; more of them jam just when you need to let go.

q: You are making the stern line fast on a pontoon cleat. Where does the line go first?
answer: Far horn first, then a turn round the base
why: Leading to the far horn first lets the base turn take the load without the line trapping itself.

q: The stern line is loaded and you need to ease it by a metre. How do you do it?
answer: Keep one turn on and let it slip round
why: The turn round the base holds the load while you ease under control.

q: You are tacking in light air and pulling the new genoa sheet in fast by hand. How many turns are on the winch?
answer: Two, adding more as the load comes on
why: Few turns let the slack come in fast without riding turns; add turns as the load builds.

q: The helm calls "Lee-oh" and you must let the old genoa sheet go. How?
answer: Pull the tail free, lift the turns off
why: Flicking the turns up off the drum releases the sheet at once so the sail can cross.

q: You are loading the sheet onto a self-tailing winch. What is the order?
answer: Clockwise turns, then over the arm into the jaws
why: The drum turns do the gripping; the jaws only hold the tail.

q: You need to ease the loaded genoa sheet a few centimetres on a plain winch. How?
answer: Keep the turns on and ease them round
why: With the turns kept on, the drum's friction lets you ease under control.

q: This line is bar taut in a gust. Where do you stand?
answer: To one side, out of line with it
why: A stretched nylon line that parts whips back along its own path.

figure.note: Nylon stern line under heavy load

q: After hoisting, you have coiled the halyard tail from this cleat. How do you hang it?
answer: Pull a loop through the coil, twist it, hang it
why: The hung coil stays tidy and lifts off ready to run.

q: You are shackling a rope warp to a length of chain. What goes inside the eye splice?
answer: A thimble, to protect the eye
why: The metal thimble spreads the load and protects the eye from chafe.

q: The marinero has done this with your stern line. Where is it adjusted and made fast?
answer: On the boat's cleat, by your crew
why: Made fast on board, the line can be adjusted or slipped without going ashore.

figure.note: Line taken round the bollard, end handed back

ru.Line taken round the bollard, end handed: Трос обнесён вокруг пала, конец вернули на борт

q: How do you rig the stern line so you can let go from on board?
answer: Both ends aboard, middle round the bollard
why: A slip line is released from aboard by letting one end go and pulling in the other.

q: You must cast off this line while the boat is still pulling on it. How?
answer: Undo the hitches while the turn holds the load
why: The round turn takes the strain while the half hitches are undone.

figure.note: Round turn and two half hitches, under load

ru.Round turn and two half hitches, under l: Круглый штык с двумя полуштыками под нагрузкой

q: You are grinding the genoa in and this is happening. What do you do?
answer: Add another turn on the drum
why: More turns give more friction; under heavy load the drum needs three or four.

figure.note: Sheet creeping round the drum, 22 kn

q: You are joining a thin line to a thick one with a sheet bend. Which line forms the U-shaped bight?
answer: The thicker line
why: The thick line makes the bight and the thin line wraps round it.

q: Your crew has long loose hair and a scarf and is about to grind the halyard winch. What do you say?
answer: Tie the hair back, tuck the scarf away
why: Hair and loose clothing can be wound into a turning drum.

q: A heavy stern line is under strain round a big bollard ashore. You must hold it, ease it under control, then cast it off with the load still on. Which hitch?
answer: Lighterman's hitch
why: The lighterman's (tugboat) hitch holds a heavy load on a post and still releases under strain.

q: Your bow line is tied to the quay ring with a bowline, and the wind presses the boat off so it is bar tight. You want to leave. What is the problem?
answer: A loaded bowline cannot be untied
why: A bowline holds well but the load must come off before it can be untied.

figure.note: Bowline, wind pressing the boat off

q: A crew member has loaded the genoa sheet like this. What happens when the sail fills?
answer: The sheet runs out round the drum
why: Yacht winches only hold one way; the turns must go on clockwise.

q: You need to put your own loop on this bollard. How?
answer: Up through their loop, then over the top
why: Dipping the eye lets either boat lift its loop off without disturbing the other.

figure.note: Another boat's loop is already on it

ru.Another boat's loop is already on it: На нём уже петля другой яхты

q: You rig a slip line through a quay ring. Your crew wants to tie a bowline in the end that will run through the ring. Why not?
answer: The knot can jam in the ring
why: A slip line must run free; any knot or eye can snag the ring.

figure.note: Slip line: both ends on board

ru.Slip line: both ends on board: Швартов на слип: оба конца на борту

q: You keep getting riding turns on this winch. How should the sheet lead onto the drum?
answer: From slightly below the drum
why: A lead from slightly below makes each new turn go on under the others.

q: You need to ease the loaded sheet on a self-tailing winch. What do you do first?
answer: Take the tail out of the jaws
why: Out of the jaws, you control the tail and the drum turns do the easing.

q: The spring and the stern line share one cleat, with the stern line on top. Why is this a problem when you leave?
answer: The spring is trapped under the stern line
why: The line underneath is trapped until the one on top is taken off.

labels: spring under, stern line on top

q: This line takes a hard snatch in a gust and parts. Where is it most likely to break?
answer: At the bowline, its weakest point
why: The tight bends in a knot weaken a rope far more than a smooth turn or a splice.

figure.note: Bowline on the bollard, cleated on board

ru.Bowline on the bollard, cleated on board: Беседочный на палу, на борту — утка
